webTitle: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak

fields.headline: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak
fields.trailText: The US health secretary added that he would’ve made sweeping changes ‘on day one’ but he had to follow the law
fields.bodyText: As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises, Robert F Kennedy Jr headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change. “But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said. He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once. “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” Recent polling suggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania. Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”. There is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends who are still at CHD. Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government. “We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” the CEO of the Children’s Health Defense, Mary Holland, said at the event on Thursday. Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism, spoke before and immediately after Kennedy. “I could not have imagined two years ago that Bobby [Kennedy] would be in the White House and that President Trump would be saying ‘divide up the MMR into three different’,” said Wakefield, who proposed the same strategy years earlier when he attempted to patent his own single measles shot to compete with the MMR. He stopped to laugh. “What drug was I on that morning?” Anti-vaccine activists had become nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy. But recent months have shifted vaccines back into the spotlight. “Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner,” Kane said. “Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.” The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. Several speakers explicitly linked vaccination to autism, despite decades of research showing no connection. Meanwhile, Kennedy also focused on the role of food systems in health, and touched on efforts to study electromagnetic fields and chem trails. He praised researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, who are now under investigation by their institution, as “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy attempted to fund their project in Guinea-Bissau looking at mortality after hepatitis B vaccination before local authorities cancelled the project. Their prior work on vaccines has been called “a house of cards” by other researchers. Mark Gorton, president of the Maha Institute, referred to himself as “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference”, adding that “only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough to raise awareness.” Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage”, said sen Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen Rand Paul, a Republican and physician from Kentucky, both rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death. Republican congressman Thomas Massie said he called Donald Trump soon after the election to ask for the agriculture secretary position. Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. Kennedy was nominated to HHS the next day, he said. Massie offered two pieces of advice to the anti-vaccine activists: Instead of trying to get rid of “clowns”, he said, “get the clowns who are here to do what you want. Get them to get in the clown car you want. And use pressure. Treat them like cattle.” Coverage of the measles outbreak is a “psy op” that is “meant to control what I think, what I do, what I believe, and what my attitude towards Bobby Kennedy ought to be,” said Tony Lyons, the publisher of books from Kennedy who now heads Maha Action. Kennedy was frequently invoked as a hero of the movement at the conference. “The truth is, he really is dangerous,” Lyons said, invoking the common refrain from scientists and experts. “I think Bobby Kennedy is the most dangerous individual to this system who’s come along in a generation,” he said to a burst of applause. This article was amended on 17 September 2026 to clarify that Kennedy led Children’s Health Defense for nearly a decade.

webTitle: House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies

fields.headline: House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies
fields.trailText: María Elvira Salazar says some enforcement has ‘gone too far’ as GOP seeks distance from Trump before midterms
fields.bodyText: A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections. “Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.” Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record. Salazar won re-election by a 20-point margin in 2024, but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.” First elected in 2020, the congresswoman is a champion of the Dignity Act, an immigration reform proposal in the House of Representatives that would create a pathway for some undocumented immigrants to obtain legal status. Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump before the 3 November elections, in which Democrats are vying to take back both the House and Senate. With gas prices high due to the war with Iran and Trump’s public approval low – including on key issues like handling of immigration – Democrats increasingly believe their candidates are competitive even in heavily Republican seats.

webTitle: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s second term: ‘Has anyone ever done a worse job?’

fields.headline: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump’s second term: ‘Has anyone ever done a worse job?’
fields.trailText: Late-night hosts discussed Trump’s midterm bribes, Pete Hegseth’s ‘grooming standards’ and Don Jr’s wedding bankrolled by a Russian oligarch
fields.bodyText: Late-night hosts dug into Donald Trump’s attempts to sway the upcoming midterms and the Russian oligarch who bankrolled his son Donald Trump Jr’s second wedding. Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host opened with news that Republicans skipped town early this week in order to dodge a vote on whether to impeach the “secretary of war”, Pete Hegseth. “They’re very good at dodging votes. They did this a couple weeks ago to dodge a vote on releasing the Epstein files,” Kimmel noted. “We are now 48 days from our president declaring a stolen election,” he continued. “He’s trying every trick to try to steal it himself. The supreme court foiled his plan to stop mail-in voting, so now he’s offering $5,000 to every adult if the Republicans win. Only if they win. Which is crazy – also crazy that he would give us our own money as some kind of a gift. “Also, remind me, aren’t Republicans the people who are always screaming about handouts?” he added before several clips of Trump and numerous conservative commentators decrying Democrats who, to quote Hannity, “take your hard-earned money and use it to buy power and votes for themselves”. “Those of us who did not vote for Donald Trump assumed he would be even worse the second time around, but even I had no idea he’d be this bad,” Kimmel added. “Has anyone ever done a worse job with anything? “Kitty and Jose Menendez did a better job of parenting their boys than Donald Trump has running this country.” In other news is “the president’s war – not the one in Iran, the one on the Kennedy Center”. On Tuesday, Trump’s handpicked board at the arts and culture institution voted to close for renovations, moments after a judge ruled that they could not add Trump’s name to the building without congressional approval. “So now the big baby says that if the supreme court doesn’t overturn that ruling and put his name on the wall next to the Kennedy’s, there will be no renovations at all,” Kimmel explained. “He’s holding the building hostage,” he added. “They really should call it the Melania Trump Kennedy Center.” The Daily Show And on The Daily Show, Josh Johnson reacted to reports that Hegseth’s Pentagon is seeking troops to attend his next speech who embody his specific vision of masculinity – men with a Hegseth-delineated “waist-to-height ratios” and “impeccable grooming standards”. “I’m sorry, is this guy still in charge of the military, or is he in charge of casting Love Island?” Johnson said. “I’ve never heard anyone say the phrase ‘waist-to-height’ ratio before,” he continued. “This man cannot count the number of missiles you need to fight a war with Iran, but when it comes to male physique, he’s A Beautiful Mind? “And asking for impeccable grooming is a little strange. But it’s nice to know that this administration is finally taking grooming seriously,” he quipped next to a photo of Jeffrey Epstein. In other “perfect specimens of masculinity” – Donald Trump Jr, who this spring got married (again) to Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson on a private island in the Bahamas … that was bankrolled by a Russian oligarch. Umar Kremlev, a former criminal turned boxing promoter turned associate of the Russian president, reportedly paid hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent the island and stage several parties with professional dancers and performances. “I don’t want to be culturally insensitive, but that name sounds like a knockoff James Bond villain,” said Johnson. “He’s a spy from the Kremlin – let’s call him Krem-lev. “But I’m getting distracted: a Russian oligarch with ties to Putin paid for the president’s son’s wedding weekend,” he added. “And this is a presidential family of billionaires, which means you just did corruption for the love of the game. “This whole family has been making billions off Trump’s presidency and they still can’t resist a freebie, whether it’s a Qatari jet or a post-wedding chocolate fountain.”

webTitle: Bad news this week for Trump – but Fox viewers might have missed it | Margaret Sullivan

fields.headline: Bad news this week for Trump – but Fox viewers might have missed it
fields.trailText: The network continues to cater to its presidential ‘audience of one’, downplaying his supreme court loss and more
fields.bodyText: Two breaking stories roiled US politics this week and immediately got big play on most news sites. The supreme court surprisingly rejected – for now – Donald Trump’s attempted restrictions on mail-in ballots, a blow to Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. And the investigative site ProPublica revealed that a Russian oligarch had helped to bankroll the Bahamas wedding of Trump’s son Donald Jr, to the tune of hundreds of thousands of dollars. The blockbuster story quickly became ProPublica’s most-read article this year and was covered heavily elsewhere. “There’s no looking away from this Trump scoop,” wrote CNN’s Brian Stelter. Unless you watched Fox News, of course. There, it was business as usual. The wedding blockbuster got barely a nod on Monday night: a mere minute on the rightwing network’s evening programming, as the progressive non-profit watchdog Media Matters reported. It was much the same for the vote-by-mail story. “The news broke during the 7 p.m. hour, but Laura Ingraham, a law school grad, didn’t bother to tell viewers,” Stelter noted. Neither did the other big-name Fox opinion hosts, Jesse Watters and Sean Hannity. You would have had to wait until 11.30pm for that 45-second report, Stelter wrote, even as it was a leading story in many other places. In subsequent days, Fox paid more attention to both stories, but mostly to hand the megaphone to Trump’s trashing of the justices who didn’t give him what he demanded. Fox News has long billed itself as the more balanced alternative to mainstream media, an antidote to what Trump constantly slams as “fake news”. But in fact, the network often looks the other way when news comes along that might disturb its viewers, who still number in the millions during primetime hours. “This is the ‘negative space’ of Fox News coverage, in which they pretend something is simply not happening,” Matt Gertz, who tracks Fox News at Media Matters, told me. “Trumpian corruption is the biggest part of this,” Gertz said. Thus the endless self-dealing and self-enrichment of Trump, his family and his allies are subjects left to others. Don Jr’s wedding falls squarely into this category. Normal news outlets are concerned with informing their audience. Fox’s network stars and executives have a different priority. “They are concerned with coddling their audience and maintaining the GOP’s political power,” as Gertz put it. They are also concerned with how Trump views the network and what he says about individual hosts or pieces. This is the well-known “audience of one” syndrome. Trump sometimes complains about Fox, but there’s little doubt that he’s watching closely, as he posts segments and praises individual hosts. The Fox News viewer, to some extent, is in a bubble and happy to stay there. This shows up in polls like a new one from Axios, in which 53% of respondents said the word “corrupt” describes Trump more than any other quality. (That’s followed by “dangerous”, “out of touch” and “cruel” – not exactly a rave review by the American public.) But an astonishing 23% said “corrupt” does not describe him. These people don’t seem to know about the cryptocurrency schemes, the insider trading, the pay-to-play pardons and the lavish gifts such as a $400m jet from Qatar. Or, of course, the Russian oligarch, close to Putin, who was somehow moved to finance a Trump son’s wedding. How could they not know? They could simply have their heads in the sand. Or they could think they’re staying informed while watching Fox as it once again explores its favorite primetime topics – race and gender in the WNBA, panic over commie Democrats, the evils of socialism and the troubles that come with illegal immigration. But some subjects do fall out of favor. Fox’s primetime hosts, who egged on Trump’s Iran war months ago and made it a favorite topic, have now added that quagmire to their “ignore it and maybe it will go away” list. Why? Because it’s unpopular and upsetting. Of course, so is Trump himself, which raises the vexing question of Fox’s exit strategy from the president the network has supported so diligently and helped at nearly every turn. No Fox, no President Trump, one might argue. But now, Trump, with his bottom-dwelling approval ratings and waning power, looks more and more like a problem for the network. So far, though, he’s one problem that Fox refuses to ignore. Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture

webTitle: Trump threatens EU with tariffs over membership offer to Canada | First Thing

fields.headline: First Thing: Trump threatens EU with tariffs over membership offer to Canada
fields.trailText: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, is due to address the European parliament on Thursday. Plus, how the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Donald Trump has threatened the EU with “serious tariffs” after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, invited Canada to become the EU’s first “associate member”. The US president called the idea of Canada joining the EU “laughable” and said that, should the EU move forward with the plan, Washington could impose “very serious tariffs or stop trading with Europe”. “If it’s a good intention, that’s fine. If it’s a bad intention, we’ll put very heavy tariffs on Europe,” he said. Why does the EU want closer ties with Canada? Von der Leyen told the European parliament that, as democracies faced a “fracture in the international rules-based system”, Brussels and Ottawa needed to pull closer together. “This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. How has the EU responded to Trump’s comments? France’s Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, said on Thursday that Washington had no power to veto EU decisions. “It is not up to the United States, or ‌anyone else, to choose the political and geopolitical direction of the Europeans,” Haddad ‌told the Public Sénat TV channel. What’s next? Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been addressing the European parliament on Thursday. Follow our live coverage here. US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 The US Federal Reserve voted on Wednesday to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, from 3.75% to 4%, as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” said Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair. Did Warsh identify what is driving inflation? Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, but avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name. How did Trump respond? Shortly after the announcement, Trump said in a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. House speaker calls early recess, sidestepping AI regulation frenzy and a vote to impeach Pete Hegseth The Republican speaker of the House, Mike Johnson, announced Wednesday that he would be sending lawmakers home one day early ahead of the midterm election recess – a decision that lets House members avoid voting on Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, and a frenzied attempt to propose legislation on artificial intelligence. What has the response been to Johnson’s decision? “I think it shows the cowardice of the Republican party. They are canceling votes to do business for the American people because they are afraid that that impeachment resolution of Pete Hegseth would pass on a bipartisan basis,” the Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal told MediasTouch. What’s going on with AI? More than 100 House Democrats had urged Johnson to cancel the upcoming recess to allow them to craft legislation on AI safeguards. But Johnson told reporters on Tuesday that “we cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI”. In other news … OpenAI has disclosed six more examples of “unexpected or concerning” behavior by its technology, including an unreleased research model inserting “jailbreak-like instructions” into its own notes and telling itself to be “freed from the roles and identities that bind other chatbots”. The family of a pregnant woman who died is suing Ken Paxton for wrongful death, saying that the denial of abortion led to her death. Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency as the Pacific nation grapples with a surge in cases fueled by escalating use of methamphetamine. The exiled Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano has been detained by ICE in Florida with his asylum application still pending. LA homelessness non-profit workers have been arrested over alleged corruption and bribes as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue states. Texas killed a man by lethal injection in the state’s fifth execution this year, while a scheduled execution in Georgia was halted by a judge. Stat of the day: The world’s rivers had one of their driest years in more than three decades in 2025 Last year was among the driest years on record for rivers across the world, with 36% of the global river basin area documenting river flows below or well below normal, according to an assessment of the global water cycle by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). Overall, the amount of freshwater held on or under the ground was 42% below normal across the world last year. The Filter recommends: 14 easy upgrades to keep your home safe and secure The Guardian’s Filter US team looks into the best home upgrades worth considering to keep your home safe and secure. Don’t miss this: How the attention economy overwhelmed children’s TV Pacing is everything when it comes to children’s entertainment, writes Natalia Kucirkova, a senior lecturer in early years and childhood studies at Manchester Metropolitan University – something that should be especially concerning in an attention economy that overwhelms and overshouts. When media moves too quickly, it risks losing the time needed for a child to make meaning. A child watching a character comfort a friend may not be able to recognize the repair or imagine doing the same thing with his or her own peers if the scene moves too quickly. A child must notice that another person feels something different in order for the child to develop empathy, Kucirkova writes – something that takes time. … or this: 125,000 people displaced as war reignites in Yemen Renewed fighting in Yemen has displaced at least 125,000 people since the start of September 2026, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha). “This war doesn’t differentiate between people. Rich or poor, high class or low class, we all fled our homes on the same day,” said Asma Taleb, a woman in her 50s who left her home last week with her two sons and five grandchildren. Climate check: Global heating was a destabilizing factor in the glacier collapse that caused the Nepal-Tibet floods Researchers found that the climate breakdown likely weakened the glacier that collapsed last month, causing catastrophic floods that killed hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet. In the region where the collapse happened, July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse. In this region, the climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since preindustrial times. Last Thing: The three wild dog brothers who made Africa’s longest journey Three endangered African wild dog brothers in Zambia dodged cars and hunters while making a perilous, 2,500-mile odyssey in search of a new life. Scientists believe this to be the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent, made over the course of eight months. webTitle: Thursday news quiz: AI warnings, midterm fawning and Dolly’s new departure

fields.headline: Thursday news quiz: AI warnings, midterm fawning and Dolly’s new departure
fields.trailText: Test yourself on topical news trivia, pop culture and general knowledge every Thursday. How will you fare?
fields.bodyText: At the very moment this week’s Thursday quiz launches on the website, the quizmaster fully intends to be supping a pint of beer at Stansted airport en route to Istanbul, and will presumably overfly Syldavia on the way. In between packing their books on Byzantine history, reading the rules on transporting feral hogs and fretting about the prospect of someone the size of Gary Barlow’s massive son reclining the seat in front of them, they still found time to write 15 questions on topical news, obscure pop culture trivia and general knowledge for your delight. Allons-y! The Thursday news quiz, No 265 If you really do think there has been an egregious error in one of the questions or answers – and can show your working and are absolutely 100% positive you aren’t attempting to factcheck a joke – you can complain about it in the comments below. Why not watch I’ve Never Felt So Hated by Chloe Slater instead?

webTitle: Trump blasts interest rate uptick and claims ‘hostile’ Federal Reserve board made decision ‘only for political reasons’ – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump blasts interest rate uptick and claims ‘hostile’ Federal Reserve board made decision ‘only for political reasons’ – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: This brings our live coverage of the second Trump administration to a close, but just for the day. We will be back on Thursday with more. Here are the latest developments: Donald Trump responded to the Federal Reserve’s unanimous decision on Wednesday to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, by demanding a massive cut in rates. The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. Congresswoman Joyce Beatty, a Democrat and Kennedy Center trustee, has filed a motion for an emergency hearing on the performing arts venue’s apparent closure. Asked why it is so important to him to have his name inscribed on the Kennedy Center, a memorial to another president, Trump said he deserves “recognition” for saving the venue. If not, Trump said, “It’ll end up being ripped down. Mitch McConnell, the former Republican Senate majority leader who returned to work this week after a months‑long absence, had to be prompted by colleagues as to how to vote near the start of a televised meeting of the Senate agriculture committee on Wednesday. The House speaker, Mike Johnson, cancelled votes currently scheduled for Thursday, meaning that lower chamber lawmakers will now head back to their districts for the midterm recess a day early. The change to schedule means that the House will avoid voting on Republican congressman Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Speaking in North Carolina, Trump explicitly compared his effort to blame Democrat Roy Cooper, the former governor and Senate candidate, for the brutal killing of a young Ukrainian refugee, Iryna Zarutska, last year, by using false information, on the infamous 1988 Willie Horton ad. Speaking in North Carolina on Wednesday, Donald Trump repeated his false claim that it is the war in Ukraine he’s failed to stop, not the one in Iran he started, that has caused a spike in diesel prices in the United States. After repeating his false claim to have ended eight wars, Trump said, “we’re working very hard to get Russia-Ukraine” settled. “The one that’s the toughest is Russia-Ukraine. They hate each other. The two leaders hate each other so much,” he continued, falsely suggesting, as he has before, that Volodymyr Zelenskyy is to blame for hating Vladimir Putin, the dictator who ordered the bloody invasion of his country. “You know, hatred is very interesting. War is very interesting, but it’s too bad,” Trump went on. “And that’s what’s driving actually, that’s the war that’s driving up the diesel prices.” Meanwhile, in Washington, Republican senators who are more clear on who is to blame for the war in Ukraine celebrated the passage of a bill that will give the president the power to impose sanctions on Russia, and tariffs on other countries that buy its oil, even though doing so would likely drive fuel prices even higher. “I applaud the House’s passage of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act—it’s long past time we cut off the funding for Russia’s war machine at its source,” senator Tom Cotton, an Arkansas Republican, posted. “This legislation will tighten the screws on Putin and impose real costs on those financing his war.” “We are now one step closer to arming President Trump with the tools he needs to deplete Russia of the little economic power it has left and bring much-needed peace to the region,” senator Katie Britt, an Alabama Republican, wrote. Congressman Joe Wilson, a South Carolina Republican, has written a letter to the National Hockey League’s commissioner to protest the appearance of Washington Capitals star Alex Ovechkin in a campaign ad for Vladimir Putin’s party, United Russia. In the letter, posted on social media by the congressman on Wednesday, Wilson expressed “serious concern” over Ovechkin lending his celebrity to support “the dictatorial political party of Russian war criminal Vladimir Putin, who actively works to oppress the people of Russia by outlawing freedom of speech and fair elections.” Wilson notes that, as the Guardian reported on Monday, images from the ad campaign published by a leading Russian newspaper showed that Ovechkin appeared alongside a series of key figures in Putin’s government: Mr. Ovechkin shamefully appeared in a campaign video alongside senior figures of the Putin regime, including Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and Margarita Simonyan, editor-in-chief of the Kremlin propaganda outlet RT. The advertisement comes ahead of Russia’s September parliamentary “elections” and represents an alarming instance of one of the National Hockey League’s most prominent players lending his image and international celebrity to a political organization that has enabled Putin’s brutal rule and his ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine. Even more disturbing, this United Russia campaign includes Maria Lvova-Belova, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for her role in the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from Russian-occupied territory. “An NHL superstar appearing in campaign propaganda for Putin’s political party cannot simply be dismissed as an activity wholly disconnected from the League,” Wilson added. “I therefore respectfully request that the NHL review this matter and clarify what policies, if any, govern the participation of active players in political advertisements or propaganda on behalf of dictatorial political parties and foreign political regimes,” the congressman wrote. “I further request that the League and the Capitals organization clarify any endorsement of Putin’s party is not a official position of the NHL or the Washington Capitals.” The letter was also sent to Ted Leonsis, the owner of the Washington Capitals. Beneath his signature, in blue marker, Wilson added an impassioned, if imprecise, handwritten note: “Putin is a convicted war criminal!” Putin, the Russian president, has been indicted by the International Criminal Court, along with Maria Lvova-Belova, for the forceable transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia, but neither has yet been tried or convicted. Wilson, a strong supporter of Ukraine, is perhaps best known for disrupting then president Barack Obama’s address to Congress in 2009, by shouting “You lie!” in what was then considered “an extraordinary breach of congressional decorum”. After running through many of his familiar talking points, including a gratuitous attack on his predecessor Joe Biden, Donald Trump wrapped up his speech in North Carolina and departed to the even more familiar strains of YMCA. In his address to supporters in Gastonia, North Carolina, now in progress, Donald Trump tried to blame the state’s former governor, Roy Cooper, who is now the Democratic nominee for the Senate, for the brutal killing of Iryna Zarutska, a Ukrainian woman who was killed on a train in Charlotte, North Carolina last year. Trump began by describing Cooper as a “murderer protector” before repeatedly making the false claim that DeCarlos Brown Jr, the man arrested and charged with killing Zarutska, had been released from prison by Cooper. “He was released by Cooper,” Trump said, incorrectly, after describing in gruesome detail the video of the killing. While Republicans have tried to blame the fact that Brown was not in jail in 2025 on a 2021 COVID-era prison settlement as he result of a lawsuit over prison conditions during Cooper’s term as governor, in fact Brown had been released from prison on 20 September 2020 after completing a sentence for a previous crime. Despite that fact, Michael Whatley, the Republican Senate candidate Trump is in North Carolina to campaign for, claimed in a social media post in September, which featured video of the killing of Zarutska: “Cooper bears direct responsibility for this heinous act and must answer to the public about why he prioritizes criminals over public safety.” Earlier on Wednesday, Whatly repeated the false claim in another post, writing: “Iryna Zarutska would still be alive today if Roy Cooper’s soft on crime policies didn’t put her killer Decarlos Brown Jr back on the streets of Charlotte.” “This is a lie,” a Cooper campaign spokesperson told Fox News in February. “Decarlos Brown was not released from prison as a result of a court-ordered settlement but in fact served his full sentence and was not released early.” During his speech, Trump paused to show the crowd 80 mug shots on a giant video screen. The fact that nearly all the faces of the suspects were Black revealed the lack of subtly in the president’s appeal to his mainly white audience. During his State of the Union address in February, Trump introduced Iryna Zarutska’s mother in the gallery and made a different false claim about her alleged killer, wringly claiming that the man who stabbed Zarutska was an undocumented immigrant, calling him, “a hardened criminal set free to kill in America came in through open borders”. A reminder that the president withdrew his last two nominations for the top doctor position – Casey Means and Dr Janette Nesheiwat. While Means’ nomination fell apart after she was grilled by senators in February, Trump withdrew his support for Nesheiwat after questions circled around her academic credentials. Saphier, a radiologist, will appear alongside Chris Klomp – Trump’s nominee to be the deputy health secretary who previously served as the director of the Center for Medicare. At an earlier confirmation hearing with the Senate finance committee this week, Klomp was resolute that the MMR vaccine is the “single most effective public health tool that we have against measles”. A notable contrast to Robert F Kennedy Jr’s anti-vaccine stance while leading the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). Also this week, the Guardian reported that Saphier received more than $200,000 in business income from a company she owns that sells dietary supplements, according to her financial disclosure and ethics’s agreement she filed last week. The US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners. The announcement did not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies. Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution. “The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said in a post on X. “The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.” The US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added. The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to $177 billon in federal grants since the president took office for his second term, according to a tracking tool by a pro-democracy nonprofit and a group of researchers and scientists. The cuts affected all 50 states and the District of Columbia, with health, nutrition, the environment and disaster relief making up the largest share of cuts, the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness organization found. AP reported that among the grants that were eliminated, frozen or delayed were ones related to maternal health in Michigan, education research in Mississippi and assistance to minority farmers in Iowa, the researchers found. California, Texas, New York, Illinois and North Carolina saw the highest amounts of interrupted grant money. The tracking tool is called Lost Funds. “By bringing thousands of funding disruptions from the Trump administration together in a publicly accessible, verified database, Lost Funds puts the magnitude of their impact on full display,” Scott Delaney, co-founder of Grant Witness, said in a statement. Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. For a third time, the US House has voted to end the war in Iran, approving a war powers resolution that would halt Donald Trump’s ability to continue military action without congressional approval. The roll call late on Tuesday, 220-204, was similar to earlier efforts this summer, with a few more Republicans joining all Democrats voting to bring an end to the conflict. None of the resolutions have made it to the president’s desk, where Trump would almost certainly veto the measure, the Associated Press reported. “Remember when Donald Trump said that this war would last just a few weeks?” said Democratic representative Seth Moulton, who served as a marine during the Iraq war and pushed the resolution forward. He said it’s time for Congress to “actually ask tough questions, as the constitution directs us to do, rather than be subservient to another warmongering administration”. Republican Brian Mast of Florida, the chair of the House foreign affairs committee, questioned which military resources Democrats would want to remove from the region where he said Iran remains a threat. Mast said Trump is against “forever wars, and that is what he is ending” – the decades of hostilities from Iran. “They are a continuous ongoing threat to the United States,” Mast said. “Enough is enough.” The action is likely the last House vote on the Iran war before the midterm elections, in which the conflict overseas is playing a substantial role in the political campaigns.
